masthead.title: Agentic commerce
masthead.contents: Three articles · Four analyses · One recommendation
masthead.standfirst: To get ahead of future scenarios we do not need omens, we need to understand the present one. In a context where artificial intelligence is starting to make decisions, designing experiences is no longer only about polishing screens. It is about earning back the trust of the person buying and the business selling, about setting limits nobody had drawn before, and about asking how far AX, the agent's experience, can go.
masthead.summary: Here we gather what we have published on the subject across our channels: what agentic design means for digital commerce, why it pushes the traditional interface towards its end, and what framework an organisation needs in order to decide before the change catches up with it.

ax.standfirst: For two decades we have chased the perfect funnel: studying how people buy and redesigning the interface again and again so they buy better. AX breaks those foundations.
ax.body: Digital commerce is shifting its focus. The challenge is no longer designing the interface but orchestrating the buying decision: what a person delegates to the agent, within which limits and under which rules. Once the agent searches, compares and pays, the shop window stops being where the sale is won.

prospectiva.standfirst: For years, organisations have reacted to noise and to trends. Today the tension lies in preparing for possibilities that have not happened yet.
prospectiva.body: Anticipating scenarios is not guessing: it is building a framework that lets you act today with clarity. Once execution is delegated to AI systems, the challenge stops being efficiency and becomes control. Preparing means deciding, with judgement, what gets automated and where human responsibility is non-negotiable.

criterio.standfirst: If an AI can generate a decent product page in seconds and an agent can buy without ever seeing it, the interface alone no longer sets us apart.
criterio.body: The ones who adapt best will not be those who master the most tools, but those who know what to ask before opening them. A look at the shift running through the craft: what has happened to the internet in recent years, what still holds from the foundations of UX, which new users are landing here, and where the design system sits now.

precedent.title: A precedent for how fast a habit can change
precedent.body: In 2020 remote work in Spain went from 5 % to 37 % in a matter of months. Not because the technology was new, but because the friction holding it back disappeared.

data.note: Adoption does not depend on technical capability alone. It depends on how impatient buyers are with friction, on regulation that will force search and purchase apart, and above all on security: nobody delegates a transaction in an environment that has not earned their explicit trust.

accesibilidad.title: The invisible screen may be the most accessible architecture ever designed
accesibilidad.body: For two decades, digital shopping has depended on the retina. For a person with a visual impairment, that has meant screen readers, badly labelled code and layers of friction. Agentic commerce can remove those barriers at the root.
points: Semantic translation. AI turns messy graphic elements into structured data a screen reader can read without ambiguity.
Voice and natural language. The system understands context, constraints and preferences with no visual navigation needed.
Invisible checkout. When the transaction happens between data interfaces, the screen stops being necessary.
accesibilidad.close: Designing the agent's experience with accessibility in mind means giving everyone back the ability to decide. Human First. Next AI.
accesibilidad.cta: Shall we help you design a more accessible world?

cero-clics.title: Zero-click purchases do not remove the decision: they move it
cero-clics.body: This is not speculation about a distant future, it is the technical consequence of delegating search, comparison and payment. For twenty years we measured success in clicks, time on page and visual funnels. In this model, the person no longer walks through the interface to buy.
points: In setting rules, budgets and preferences.
In defining how far the agent may act on its own.
In how much trust it is granted.
cero-clics.close: Most digital shops are still built on the inertia of the visual shop window. If your catalogue attributes and your offer conditions are not legible to an agent, your shop falls outside the delegated purchase flow.
cero-clics.cta: Is your business ready for that shift?

invisibilidad.title: How products turn invisible under an agent's gaze
invisibilidad.body: Who evaluates and selects has changed. Once search is delegated to an autonomous assistant, the recommendation no longer rests on the shop window but on how precise the information is.
points: Language models do not read metaphors or corporate slogans: they ignore them.
Ambiguity is a blind spot. With no concrete attributes or clear limits, the system drops the offer.
The algorithm will always favour the competitor with the sharper information.
invisibilidad.close: Being recommended takes rigour: explaining what the product does, how it is made and the conditions under which it works. People and algorithms both need to understand the proposition.
invisibilidad.cta: If an assistant scanned your catalogue today, would it find clear data?
invisibilidad.imageAlt: A grid of sixteen shop mannequins: fourteen on near-identical beige and grey backgrounds, and only two on saturated colour.
invisibilidad.imageCaption: Fourteen of sixteen shop windows are the same shop window. To an agent, indistinguishable.

adopcion.title: From signals to scenarios
adopcion.body: We already delegate operational work, our calendars and data analysis. Buyers are internalising that delegating cognitive tasks reduces friction, and the buying decision is the logical next step. Trust moves from the shop to the algorithm doing the filtering.
adopcion.close: With strategic foresight we turn those signals into plausible scenarios. That lets an organisation reduce uncertainty, prepare the cultural shift and order its decisions before scaling.
adopcion.cta: Is your organisation ready for this new way of buying?

recommends.title: Historia Ficción
recommends.body: This episode imagines a twenty-second-century society organised around abundance. It runs through three revolutions, the Neolithic, the Industrial and the Information one, to ask what happens when automation, cheap energy and software stop fitting the economic rules we know. The value is in the exercise: using history to design futures and to question what we take as inevitable. In Spanish.

close.title: The buying decision is already moving.
close.body: You do not need to pick the exact scenario to be ready. You need to know what gets automated, where responsibility stays human, and whether your catalogue can be understood by someone who no longer looks at screens.
